item.title: The Office Ratings
item.dc:creator: John Donnellan
item.description:
Introduction:

This dataset contains information on all 188 episodes of The Office, beginning with the pilot episode in 2005 and ending with the series finale in 2013. The show spans nine seasons and provides a useful dataset for examining trends in episode ratings over time. In this analysis, I will explore how IMDb ratings vary across seasons and identify notable outliers, including episodes that received particularly high or low ratings.

Research Question:

How do IMDb ratings and audience engagement (measured by total votes) vary across seasons of The Office?

Link to the data set: https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/blob/main/data/2020/2020-03-17/readme.md

The Variables:

  • season: Season number

  • episode: Episode number

  • title: Title of the episode

  • imdb_rating: IMDB rating of the episode on a scale from 1–10 (10 is best)

  • total_votes: Total number of votes submitted by IMDB users

  • air_date: Original air date of the episode

Loading the Data:

library(tidyverse)
library(readr)
office_ratings <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2020/2020-03-17/office_ratings.csv')

office_ratings <- office_ratings |>
  mutate(season = factor(season))

Graph 1:

ggplot(office_ratings, aes(x = season, y = imdb_rating, color = season)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = mean(office_ratings$imdb_rating),
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = .8,
    color = "darkgrey"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Season",
    y = "IMDB Rating",
    color = "Season",
    title = "Distribution of Office Episode Ratings by Season",
    caption = "The dashed horizontal line represents the overall mean IMDb rating across all episodes."
  )+
  theme_minimal()

Interpretation:

The boxplot shows that episode ratings for The Office are highest in the middle seasons, particularly Seasons 3–5, where the median ratings are above about 8.5. In contrast, the later seasons, Seasons 8 and 9 have lower median ratings, indicating a decline in audience reception toward the end of the series. The three highest-rated episodes are “Goodbye, Michael” (Season 7) and “Finale” (Season 9), both rated 9.7, along with “Stress Relief” (Season 5) at 9.6, which stand out as clear outliers. On the other hand, the lowest-rated episodes “Get the Girl” (Season 8) with a 6.7 rating, “The Banker” (Season 6) at 6.8, and “Gettysburg” (Season 8) at 7.0 fall well below the typical range.

Graph 2:

ggplot(office_ratings, aes(x = episode, y = imdb_rating, color = season)) +
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE)+
  facet_wrap(~season) +
    labs(
    x = "Episode Number",
    y = "IMDB Rating",
    color = "Season",
    title = "Episode Rating Trends by Season")+
    theme(legend.position = "none")

Interpretation:

This faceted plot shows how IMDb ratings change across episodes within each season of The Office. Seasons 2 through 5 generally maintain consistently high ratings, suggesting these seasons represent the strongest and most stable period of the show. Beginning around Season 6, the ratings begin to vary and tend to trend slightly downward, with Seasons 8 and 9 showing the lowest overall ratings across their episodes. However, Season 9 ends with a sharp increase in ratings for the final episodes in the highly rated series finale.

Graph 3:

ggplot(office_ratings, aes(x = total_votes, y = season, color = season)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    x = "Votes",
    y = "Season",
    title = "Distribution of Votes by Season"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

Interpretation:

This boxplot shows the distribution of IMDb vote counts for The Office episodes across each season. Most episodes across all seasons receive between roughly 1,500 and 2,500 votes, though several seasons contain outliers with significantly higher votes. The most voted episodes are “Finale” (Season 9) with 7,934 votes, “Stress Relief” (Season 5) with 5,948 votes, and “Goodbye, Michael” (Season 7) with 5,749 votes, all of which appear as extreme outliers.

Conclusion and Wrap-Up

Overall, the ratings of The Office tend to be strongest during the middle seasons. In contrast, the later seasons show lower median ratings and greater variability, suggesting a decline in audience reception toward the end of the series. Despite this, several episodes stand out, including “Goodbye, Michael,” “Stress Relief,” and the series finale, which receive both extremely high ratings and large numbers of votes. One limitation of this analysis is that it relies only on IMDb ratings and vote counts, which reflect viewer opinions but do not capture other factors such as other critical reviewers.

Connection to Class Ideas

The boxplots illustrate the distribution and variation in episode ratings across seasons, making it easier to compare medians and identify outliers. The faceted episode plots allow patterns within each season to be viewed clearly while keeping the visualization organized. These visuals also use a combination of coloring, faceting, and trendlines to portray multiple variables without making the graphs look confusing or cluttered, which helps communicate the relationships in the data more effectively.

item.title: Wine Ratings by Variety and Origin
item.dc:creator: John Donnellan
item.description:
Introduction:

This analysis uses a wine review dataset obtained from Kaggle, which contains detailed reviews of wines from various countries, and grape varieties around the world. After cleaning the data, the dataset includes over 12,000 observations, each with information on the wine’s origin, grape variety, price, and rating.

How does the country of origin, variety of grape, and price affect the overall rating of the wine?

Link to data set: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/zynicide/wine-reviews

The Variables:

  • country: Country of origin

  • points: Number of points WineEnthusiast rated the wine on a scale of 1-100

  • price: The cost for a bottle of the wine

  • variety: Grape type

Loading and Cleaning the Data:

library(tidyverse)
library(readr)
wine_ratings <- readr::read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2019/2019-05-28/winemag-data-130k-v2.csv")

wine <- wine_ratings |>
  filter(!is.na(price)) |>
  filter(!is.na(country)) |>
  filter(!is.na(variety)) |>
  filter(!is.na(province)) |>
  select(country, points, price, variety, province)|>
  arrange(desc(price)) |>
  slice(-(1:100))

The dataset was first cleaned by removing observations with missing values for price, country, variety, and province to ensure that all variables used in the analysis were complete. We then selected only the relevant variables and removed the 100 most expensive wines, as these extreme price outliers were skewing the mean price and distorting comparisons across countries and varieties.

Graph #1

wine |>
  group_by(variety) |>
  filter(n() > 3000) |>
  summarize(
    avg_price = mean(price),
    avg_points = mean(points)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = avg_price, y = avg_points, color = variety)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Average Price vs Average Rating by Grape Variety",
    subtitle = "Includes grape varieties with more than 3,000 reviews",
    x = "Average Price",
    y = "Average Rating",
    color = "Grape Variety"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Interpretation:

This scatterplot shows a positive relationship between average price and average rating across grape varieties, though the relationship is modest. Higher priced varieties such as Pinot Noir and Syrah tend to have higher average ratings, clustered near the top of the graph. In contrast, lower priced wines like Rosé and Merlot sit toward the lower end of the rating scale, though the differences in average points are smaller overall.

Graph #2

overall_avg <- mean(wine$points)

wine |>
  group_by(country) |>
  filter(n() > 400) |>
  mutate(avg_price = mean(price),
         avg_points = mean(points)) |>
  ungroup()|>
  mutate(country = fct_reorder(country, avg_points)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = country, y = points, fill = avg_price)) +
  geom_boxplot()+
  geom_hline(yintercept = overall_avg, linetype = "dashed")+
  scale_fill_viridis_b() +
  labs(
    title = "Wine Ratings by Country",
    subtitle = "Countries with More Than 400 Wines",
    x = "Country",
    y = "Points",
    fill = "Average Price") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 0.5))

Interpretation:

This boxplot compares the distribution of wine ratings across countries with more than 400 reviewed wines, with color indicating each country’s average price binned into $5 increments. While there is some variation in median ratings, most countries cluster between roughly 86 and 90 points, suggesting that overall quality is relatively consistent among countries. Countries with higher average prices do not always have higher average ratings, indicating that price alone does not guarantee more points.

Graph #3

overall_avg <- mean(wine$points)

wine |>
  group_by(variety) |>
  filter(n() > 1200) |>
  mutate(
    avg_points = mean(points),
    avg_price = mean(price)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(variety = fct_reorder(variety, avg_points)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = points, y = variety, fill = avg_price)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = overall_avg, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  labs(
    title = "Wine Ratings by Grape Variety",
    subtitle = "Dashed line shows overall average rating",
    x = "Points",
    y = "Grape Variety",
    fill = "Average Price"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Interpretation:

This boxplot shows the distribution of ratings for grape varieties with more than 1,200 reviews, ordered by their average rating and colored by average price. Varieties such as Nebbiolo and Champagne Blend appear above the overall average rating (dashed line), indicating stronger ratings for expensive varieties. In contrast, varieties like Rose, Merlot, and White Blend tend to fall below the overall mean, though their distributions still overlap heavily with higher-rated types.

Conclusion and Wrap-Up

Overall, price, country of origin, and grape variety all show some relationship with wine ratings, but none appear to strongly determine quality on their own. Higher-priced wines and certain varieties tend to receive slightly higher average ratings, though the differences are relatively small. One limitation of this analysis is the removal of the 100 most expensive wines, which may exclude meaningful high-end observations while reducing skew.

Connection to Class Ideas

These visualizations apply key ideas from class about effective data communication. Ordering categories by average rating improves clarity and makes comparisons easier, while boxplots display the variation rather than relying only on means. The reference lines provide context for interpreting above and below average ratings. Additionally, color encoding allows an extra variable (average price) to be shown without making the visualizing.

item.title: Pixar Film Ratings
item.dc:creator: John Donnellan
item.description:
Introduction:

I am working with the Pixar film data set posted from TidyTuesday 2025-03-11. The data comes from the {pixarfilms} R package by Eric Luang. There are 23 observations in this data set. I am most interested in observing the differences in ratings between the main stream critics by Rotten Tomatoes, Meta Critics, and Critics Choice.

The variables I will be examining:

  • ratings: Name of rating source (Rotten Tomatoes, Meta Critics, and Critics Choice)

  • avg_rating: The average rating given on a particular movie by each of the three rating sources

  • value: The score out of a hundred given by Rotten Tomatoes, Meta Critics, and Critics Choice

  • period: Whether the movie was released before or after 2010

  • film: The title of the film

Loading the Data:

library(dplyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(pixarfilms)
pixar_films <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-03-11/pixar_films.csv')
public_response <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-03-11/public_response.csv')


pixar <-
  public_response %>%
  left_join(box_office, by = "film") %>%
  left_join(pixar_films, by = "film") %>%
  group_by(film) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c("rotten_tomatoes", "metacritic", "critics_choice"),
               names_to = "ratings",
               values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(ratings = case_when(
    ratings == "metacritic" ~ "Metacritic",
    ratings == "rotten_tomatoes" ~ "Rotten Tomatoes",
    ratings == "critics_choice" ~ "Critics Choice"
  )) %>%
  select(-cinema_score, - budget ) %>%
  drop_na()%>%
  mutate(avg_rating = mean(value)) %>%
  mutate( period = if_else(release_date <= as.Date("2009-12-31"),"Before 2010","2010 and After"), 
          # I got some help from the web to transform the release date to organize films by year,
    period = fct_relevel(period, c("Before 2010", "2010 and After")))%>%
  arrange(desc(avg_rating))

Graph #1

  ggplot(data = pixar, aes(x =fct_reorder(film, avg_rating), y = value, col = ratings)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(aes(group = ratings)) +
  scale_color_viridis_d() +
  labs(x = "Pixar film", y = "Rating value", title = "Ratings by Film") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 0.5))

Interpretation:

This graph shows Pixar films ordered from lowest to highest average rating, with scores from Rotten Tomatoes, Metacritic, and Critics Choice plotted for each movie. While Rotten Tomatoes generally gives higher scores and Metacritic gives lower ones, all three sources move together across films. This indicates strong agreement among critics about which Pixar movies are better or worse, even if they use slightly different scoring standards.

Graph #2

ggplot(data = pixar, aes(y = value, x = ratings, color = ratings))+
  geom_boxplot()+
  scale_color_viridis_d() +
  labs(x = "Ratings", y = "Value", color = "Ratings", title = "Distribution of Ratings by Source")+
   theme(legend.position = "none")

Interpretation:

This boxplot compares the overall distribution of ratings from Critics Choice, Metacritic, and Rotten Tomatoes. Rotten Tomatoes has the highest median rating, suggesting it is the most generous source, while Metacritic has the lowest median and the widest spread, indicating stricter and more variable scoring. Critics Choice falls between the two in both typical score and variability. The presence of lower outlier Cars 2 with an average rating of approximately 55.

Graph #3

ggplot(pixar, aes(x = period, y = value, fill = period)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~ ratings) +
  labs(x = "Release Period", y = "Value", title = "Before vs After 2010 by Rating Source") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

Interpretation:

This graph compares ratings before and after 2010 separately for each rating source. For all three sources, the median rating is higher for films released before 2010, suggesting Pixar’s earlier movies were more consistently well received. The post-2010 period shows greater spread and lower minimum values, especially for Metacritic and Rotten Tomatoes. Overall, this indicates that more recent Pixar films have had more mixed and less consistently strong critical reception.

Stat 334 Connection:

These visualizations are effective because they use they rely on different graphs using position, grouping, and faceting to make differences across rating sources and time periods easy to see. The visuals eliminate clutter, and focus attention as appropriate to answer my question of interest: What are the differences in ratings between the main stream critics by Rotten Tomatoes, Meta Critics, and Critics Choice.

Conclusion:

Across these visualizations, all three rating sources show a similar pattern from movie to movie. However, Rotten Tomatoes consistently rates higher scores, while Metacritic tends to rate the same films more conservatively. This suggests that although the sources differ in their scoring standards, they largely agree on which movies are better or worse.

One limitation of this analysis is that it is based on only 23 Pixar films, which means individual movies and outliers can have a large influence on the patterns we observe. The data also only three critic sources even though they each use different scoring standards. In addition, the graphs only show the differences but cannot describe why the differences occur. If I could do this again I would find a data set of all animated movies to see how the different rating sources grade for different companies.
